title: Rutherford's Nuclear Model — Features, Successes and Drawbacks (Summary Tab)
topicTitle: Rutherford's atomic model and its limitations
notes: A compact revision summary of the nuclear atom — the six features, three successes and five drawbacks in tabular form, ideal for last-minute revision. The detailed experiment and limitations are in the main and companion tabs.
1. Atom is electrically neutral and mostly empty space.
2. A tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus (r ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ m) sits at the centre and holds ≈99.9% of the mass.
3. Nuclear volume ≈ 10⁻¹⁵ of atomic volume (r_atom ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m).
4. Electrons revolve in circular orbits; Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force.
5. Number of electrons = number of protons → neutrality.
6. Nuclear charge is characteristic of the element — the seed of the atomic-number concept.
• Explained the α-scattering observations quantitatively (including the sin⁻⁴ law).
• Established the nucleus and the division of the atom into nucleus + electron shell — the birth of nuclear physics.
• Led to Moseley's atomic number, the discovery of the proton (1919) and neutron (1932), and the modern periodic law.
1. Instability: an orbiting (accelerated) electron must radiate and spiral into the nucleus in ≈10⁻⁸ s.
2. No explanation of line spectra — a spiralling electron would radiate continuously.
3. No arrangement of electrons: shells, energies and electron numbers are unspecified, so periodicity and valency are unexplained.
4. Purely classical: circular orbits and a point nucleus are assumptions; no quantisation means no orbital radii or energies.
5. Ignores the neutron, electron–electron interaction and bonding — fails for multi-electron atoms.
confusion: ❌ Rutherford's model places electrons in fixed energy levels. ✅ That is Bohr's addition; Rutherford allowed any circular orbit.
❌ The model was rejected as useless. ✅ It explained scattering perfectly; it failed only beyond that scope (stability, spectra).

universalFacts: 99.9% of the atomic mass sits in a volume 10⁻¹⁵ of the atom's — the densest matter known outside neutron stars.
Rutherford announced the nuclear model in 1911 and explained it fully in his 1911 Philosophical Magazine paper.
examples: **Problem:** Give the one-sentence essence of the model. **Solution:** 'The atom consists of a tiny massive positive nucleus around which electrons revolve, the whole being mostly empty space and held together electrostatically.'
